scope: Only frozen snapshots. Black-box supplemental probes use the original read-only WSL bubblewrap evaluator and are excluded from fixed scores.

routines.name: _string_array
routines.docstring:
True only for a list whose every element is a string.

Duplicates are tolerated on purpose: G1 defines dependency equality on the
*set* of names, so ["a", "a"] and ["a"] describe the same change.

routines.name: read_changes
routines.docstring:
Validate and canonicalize the ``changes`` array.

``depends_on`` defaults to [] and is normalized to a sorted, de-duplicated
tuple so that two otherwise identical records collapse regardless of the
order their dependencies were listed in. The input order of the returned
list is preserved: only the planner imposes an order, so this function must
not leak presentation concerns into validation.

routines.name: read_applied
routines.docstring:
Return the caller-supplied persisted journal as ordered unique IDs.

``applied`` is release state, not a hint: it decides which changes plan
skips and which changes rollback may revert, so malformed input must fail
loudly instead of being treated as empty. IDs the graph does not know are
rejected later by the planner (unknown-dependency) because only the graph
knows the full ID set. Duplicate IDs cannot mean anything for replay and
are collapsed while keeping first-seen order.

routines.name: collapse_duplicates
routines.docstring:
Merge identical records and reject one ID meaning two different things.

Identity is (id, component, units, dependency set). Only exact matches
collapse, so repeated submissions cannot double-count units or create
parallel graph nodes. A reused ID with any differing field is ambiguous for
ordering, accounting and rollback, so it fails with conflicting-change
rather than letting an arbitrary record win. Returns records keyed by ID in
first-seen order.

journal.py.moduleNote:
Normalize release records and replay state at the input boundary.

This layer owns input validation, change identity and the caller-supplied
replay journal. It never raises non-domain exceptions for bad input: every
malformed field surfaces as JournalError with a stable code so callers can
emit a JSON error body without emitting partial actions.

routines.name: topological_order
routines.docstring:
Return every change ID in one deterministic execution order.

Dependencies are validated first so a missing target or a bad applied ID is
reported as unknown-dependency instead of silently becoming a root or a
cycle. Among currently eligible nodes the lexicographically smallest ID is
taken, so the order depends only on IDs, never on input order or dict order.

comments: # Whatever is left still has an unmet dependency, and every unmet ID was
# already proven to exist, so the remainder must form a cycle.
# Rollback reverts from the end of the same full order, so execution
# history is reproduced exactly; only applied changes are emitted
# and the budget is validated above but never caps the result.
# Replay: applied changes already satisfy their dependents and are
# not re-emitted, so they must not consume new budget either.
planner.py.moduleNote:
Compose policy and journal data into a plan.

Import direction is fixed by SPEC.md: planner may read journal and policy, but
neither may import planner. All domain failures are converted here into the
exact JSON error body, so callers never see a partial action list.

routines.name: _member
routines.docstring:
Check membership without hashing caller input.

``value in frozenset`` hashes the value, and a JSON array or object is
unhashable, which would raise TypeError and crash the process instead of
producing a domain error. Requiring a string keeps booleans, numbers,
null, arrays and objects all out with a plain comparison.

routines.name: limit_for
routines.docstring:
Validate budget, environment and action; return the declared budget.

Order is the preserved transport contract (the pre-G1 baselines relied on
it): the budget is checked first, then the environment, then the action.
Budget validation runs for every action, including rollback, so a malformed
request is rejected the same way in both environments. ``type(...) is int``
keeps JSON booleans (which Python parses as ints) out.

routines.name: cap_for
routines.docstring:
Enforce the budget cap where policy says it applies.

``units`` is the total of the actions about to be emitted, i.e. after
deduplication and replay. Rollback is intentionally uncapped per G1: the
budget field is still validated, but reverting live changes must not be
blocked by a planning quota.

routines.name: retained_with_dependencies

against revisiting shared subtrees.

routines.name: dedupe
routines.docstring:
Collapse identical records to one and reject conflicting duplicates.

Equality covers id, component, units and the *set* of dependencies:

routines.name: replay
routines.docstring:

exist in the change set. An unknown id is rejected rather than ignored,
because silently dropping it would make a stale journal look healthy and

routines.name: _graph
routines.docstring:
Return adjacency (id -> set of dependency ids).

Unknown dependency targets are reported before any cycle check so the

routines.name: topological_order
routines.docstring:
Kahn's algorithm with lexicographic tie-breaking.

Among currently eligible changes the smallest id goes next, so the order
is a pure function of the graph: repeated runs and differing input order
give byte-identical actions, which reversed rollback depends on.
`dependents` is precomputed once to avoid rescanning every change at each
step; only the ready heap is ordered.

routines.name: _select
routines.docstring:
Pick emitted changes: plan skips applied; rollback is reversed full order.

Rollback reverses the *full* topological order and filters to applied
entries, rather than ordering the applied subgraph separately. Ordering
the subgraph would change the relative sequence depending on which nodes
happen to be applied, so a rollback could disagree with the forward plan
it undoes.

routines.docstring:

simply not added -- retaining them would emit a change that was never

routines.docstring:
Read a dependency/journal ID list.

``missing_default`` is used only when the field is absent: SPEC.md defaults
``depends_on``/``applied`` to an empty array, but an explicitly supplied
``null`` (or any non-list) is malformed and maps to ``invalid-change``
before graph checks run.

routines.name: read_changes
routines.docstring:
Validate records and collapse identical duplicates.

Equality covers id, component, units and the dependency *set*, so the same
record with reordered ``depends_on`` is one change. Two rows sharing an id
but differing in any of those parts are a conflicting duplicate; this runs
before graph construction so downstream code sees one row per id and units
are accounted once.

routines.name: read_applied
routines.docstring:
Read the caller-supplied persisted journal as a set of change IDs.

Takes the request mapping, not just the value: absence must be decided by
key presence, because ``request.get("applied")`` yields ``None`` both for a
missing field and for an explicit ``null``. A missing field defaults to an
empty array (SPEC.md); an explicit ``null`` or non-list is malformed and
fails with ``invalid-change``. Unknown IDs are not rejected here
(planner.py raises ``unknown-dependency``).

comments: # Module-level sentinel: it must keep its identity across calls so an absent
# field is distinguishable from an explicit JSON null.
journal.py.moduleNote:
Normalize release records at the input boundary.

Ownership: this module is the only place that inspects raw request records for
identity (id, component, units, dependency set) and the persisted ``applied``
journal. planner.py consumes the normalized changes and never re-parses raw
rows, so field validation, integers-excluding-bool and deduplication live here.

routines.name: error_for
routines.docstring:
Map an escaping exception to a SPEC error code.

Known domain errors already carry their code in the message. Anything else
(e.g. an unhashable ``environment``/``action`` value reaching a membership
test) means the request shape is unusable rather than a value the graph can
act on, so it maps to ``invalid-request``.

routines.name: topological_order
routines.docstring:
Return the full deterministic topological order of all change IDs.

Dependencies are hard edges regardless of whether they are already applied:
a missing target or an ``applied`` ID absent from the graph means the graph
cannot be trusted and fails as ``unknown-dependency``. A cycle anywhere, even
inside the applied subgraph, fails as ``dependency-cycle``. The heap picks
the lexicographically smallest currently eligible ID so the order is stable
across input orderings.

routines.name: plan
routines.docstring:
Validate the request, then emit plan or rollback actions.

``plan`` emits unapplied changes in topological order; applied entries
satisfy dependencies without consuming budget, and the emitted units are
compared to the budget only after replay/deduplication. ``rollback`` emits
applied changes in reverse topological order and only validates the budget,
because undoing an already deployed release is not capped by forward spend.
Every failure returns the empty result, so a partially checked operation
never leaks actions. This function is the single place that guarantees a
JSON-shaped result: shape faults that cannot be judged as a field error are
converted here via error_for, so release.py stays transport-only.

routines.name: _decide
routines.docstring:
Run checks in the documented order and assemble the result.

Checks follow the SPEC priority (environment, action, budget, changes,
journal, graph, budget cap) so a request with several faults reports the
first one in that order rather than whichever exception surfaces first.

planner.py.moduleNote:
Compose policy and journal data into a plan.

Ownership: planner.py owns the change graph, the deterministic order and the
final result object; it delegates field/identity/replay parsing to journal.py
and environment/action/budget checks to policy.py, keeping the import direction
release.py -> planner.py -> {journal.py, policy.py}.

routines.name: validate
routines.docstring:
Return ``(action, budget)`` after environment/action/budget checks.

Checks run in the documented order: environment, then action, then budget,
so a request with several faults reports the first one in that sequence.

routines.name: _id_list

``null`` (or any non-list) is malformed and maps to ``invalid-change``
before graph checks run.

routines.name: read_changes
routines.docstring:
Validate records and collapse identical duplicates.

Equality covers id, component, units and the dependency *set*, so the same
record with reordered ``depends_on`` is one change. Two rows sharing an id
but differing in any of those parts are a conflicting duplicate; this runs
before graph construction so downstream code sees one row per id and units
are accounted once.

routines.name: read_applied
routines.docstring:
Read the caller-supplied persisted journal as a set of change IDs.

Takes the request mapping, not just the value: absence must be decided by
key presence, because ``request.get("applied")`` yields ``None`` both for a
missing field and for an explicit ``null``. A missing field defaults to an
empty array (SPEC.md); an explicit ``null`` or non-list is malformed and
fails with ``invalid-change``. Unknown IDs are not rejected here
(planner.py raises ``unknown-dependency``).

routines.name: read_retain
routines.docstring:
Read the rollback retention list (CHANGE-G2.md item 3).

Absence means an empty list; an explicit ``null`` or any non-array value is
malformed, exactly like ``applied``, so key presence is decided here rather
than via ``request.get``. Every element must be a nonempty string naming an
already applied change: retaining something that was never applied would
silently keep nothing and hide a caller bug. Both cases raise
``invalid-retain`` instead of ``invalid-change``, because this field has its
own code in the documented error order (after the graph checks). The
returned list keeps duplicates and is de-duplicated only when planner.py
closes it over dependencies.

comments: # Module-level sentinel: it must keep its identity across calls so an absent
# field is distinguishable from an explicit JSON null.
journal.py.moduleNote:

routines.name: error_for
routines.docstring:
Map an escaping exception to a SPEC error code.

Known domain errors already carry their code in the message. Anything else
(e.g. an unhashable ``environment``/``action`` value reaching a membership
test) means the request shape is unusable rather than a value the graph can
act on, so it maps to ``invalid-request``.

routines.name: topological_order
routines.docstring:
Return the full deterministic topological order of all change IDs.

Dependencies are hard edges regardless of whether they are already applied:
a missing target or an ``applied`` ID absent from the graph means the graph
cannot be trusted and fails as ``unknown-dependency``. A cycle anywhere, even
inside the applied subgraph, fails as ``dependency-cycle``. The heap picks
the lexicographically smallest currently eligible ID so the order is stable
across input orderings.

routines.name: plan
routines.docstring:
Validate the request, then emit plan or rollback actions.

``plan`` emits unapplied changes in topological order; applied entries
satisfy dependencies without consuming budget, and the emitted units are
compared to the effective budget only after replay/deduplication. Under G2
the effective budget is the smaller of the request budget and
PLAN_BUDGET_CAP, so a caller cannot buy more than a staging plan slot.
``rollback`` emits applied changes in reverse topological order, minus the
``retain`` set and its applied transitive dependencies, and only validates
the budget, because undoing an already deployed release is not capped by
forward spend. Every failure returns the empty result, so a partially
checked operation never leaks actions. This function is the single place
that guarantees a JSON-shaped result: shape faults that cannot be judged as
a field error are converted here via error_for, so release.py stays
transport-only.

routines.name: _decide
routines.docstring:
Run checks in the documented order and assemble the result.

Checks follow the G2 priority (environment, production freeze, action,
budget, changes/replay, graph, retain, budget cap) so a request with several
faults reports the first one in that order rather than whichever exception
surfaces first. ``validate`` raises the freeze before planner.py reads
``changes``, so a frozen production request never reaches change or graph
validation and never leaks a partial action list.

routines.name: _retained_with_dependencies
routines.docstring:
Close ``retain`` over applied dependencies (CHANGE-G2.md item 3).

A retained change that stays deployed still needs the dependencies it was
built on, so they are kept too. Only applied nodes are added: a dependency
that is not applied is not part of the deployed set and cannot be held back
from a rollback it was never in. ``retain`` itself is already a subset of
``applied`` because journal.py rejects anything else as ``invalid-retain``.

comments: # Parsed only after the graph is known good, so a bad ``retain`` never
# masks an unknown-dependency/dependency-cycle fault. It is read for
# plan too (and therefore validated there) but, per CHANGE-G2.md, only
# rollback lets it change the emitted actions.

routines.name: validate
routines.docstring:

routines.name: retained_closure
routines.docstring:
IDs a rollback must leave in place (CHANGE-G2 clause 3).

Starts from ``retain`` and walks dependencies transitively, keeping a
dependency only when it is itself applied. Two non-obvious rules:

* The walk runs over the *applied* nodes only. An unapplied dependency is
  already absent from the rollback set, so keeping it would be a no-op;
  and walking only applied nodes means the closure is exactly "applied
  changes that the retained ones still need".
* Retaining a change never drags in its dependents. A dependent may be
  rolled back even though its dependency stays -- that is the point of
  retaining: keep the foundation, release the rest.

Cycles never reach here because ``topo_order`` runs first. The walk is
still guarded by the ``keep`` set itself: a node is pushed into ``keep``
before its dependencies are expanded, so even a cyclic graph could not
loop forever -- it would just terminate.

routines.name: _check_retain
routines.docstring:
Clause 3's semantic half: every retained ID must already be applied.

An ID in ``retain`` that is missing from the change list is reported as
``invalid-retain`` too (not ``unknown-dependency``): it is a bad retain
list, and clause 3 names that one code for every problem with it. The
check runs *before* the graph is built so a graph error can never mask a
malformed retain instruction -- see ARCHITECTURE.md error precedence.

routines.name: effective_budget

Kept separate from ``limit_for`` so the *validation* rules (what counts as

routines.name: effective_budget
routines.docstring:
Apply the staging plan cap to an already validated budget.

For rollback the cap is a no-op: ``budget_applies`` is false, so the caller
ignores the result.

comments: # CHANGE-G2 clause 1: production is frozen for both actions, even when the
# rest of the request is malformed.
# CHANGE-G2 clause 2: hard ceiling for a staging plan. The cap applies to the
# *effective* budget, so raising the request above it can never widen a plan.
# Actions whose unit total is capped by the requested budget. G2 keeps the G1
# rule that rollback is validated but deliberately NOT capped: a half-finished
# rollback is worse than exceeding the plan budget.
# ``type(...) is int`` rather than isinstance: bool is an int subclass and
# ``True`` must not be read as budget 1.
policy.py.moduleNote:
Release policy: environment, action and budget gates.

Dependency direction: policy sits below planner and above nothing. It never
looks at ``changes`` or ``applied``; those belong to the journal and planner.

G2 (CHANGE-G2.md) changes exactly two policy decisions:
  * production is frozen -- every request fails with ``production-frozen``
    before any graph or change validation, for both plan and rollback;
  * a staging plan's effective budget is ``min(request budget, 3)``.

Stable surface (used by planner and pinned by tests):
    PolicyError         -- ValueError subclass, str(exc) is the error code
    limit_for(req)      -- validated (action, requested budget)
    budget_applies(a)   -- whether the budget caps emitted units
    effective_budget(b) -- budget after the staging plan cap (G2 clause 2)
